blocks.text: 1. Sharding

blocks.alt: Partitions distribute across machine 1 and machine 2

blocks.text: Sharding covers how partitions get distributed across multiple machines, giving the distributed case its own full treatment.
It spreads a collection's data across separate physical servers, a distributed scaling strategy.
2. From Logical To Physical Distribution
Partitioning splits data logically; sharding takes that split and spreads it physically.
Each shard lives on its own separate machine, not just a separate section of one machine.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Concept","Where data lives"],"rows":[["Partitioning","Logical splits, potentially on one machine"],["Sharding","Physical splits, spread across multiple machines"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Why One Machine Eventually Runs Out

blocks.alt: Data keeps growing beyond one machine capacity

blocks.text: Any single machine has a hard ceiling on memory, storage, and compute.
A collection that outgrows one machine has no choice but to spread across several.
4. Shard Key Selection

blocks.alt: A shard key gives even distribution across shards

blocks.text: The same key selection principles from choosing partition keys apply here, now with physical machine placement at stake.
A poor shard key can overload one machine while others sit underused.
5. Query Coordination Across Shards

blocks.alt: A query reaches shard 1 and shard 2

blocks.text: A query touching multiple shards needs a coordinator to fan out the request and merge results.
That coordination step adds real complexity compared to a single machine search.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A coordinator handling a broad query sends that query to every relevant shard in parallel, waits for each shard's partial results, and merges them into one final, ranked result set.

blocks.text: 6. Network Latency Between Shards

blocks.alt: Shard A reaches shard B through a network hop

blocks.text: Shards living on separate machines communicate over a network, not local memory.
That network hop adds latency that a single machine search never had to pay.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: A query that touches ten shards spread across a network takes at least as long as its slowest single shard response, so an unevenly loaded or distant shard can drag down the whole query's latency.

blocks.text: 7. Fault Tolerance Across Shards
One shard's machine failing only affects the data living on that specific shard.
The rest of the collection can keep serving queries normally.
8. Sharding Versus Replication

blocks.alt: Sharding splits data while replication copies data

blocks.text: Sharding splits different data across machines.
Replication instead copies the same data across machines, a complementary but different strategy covered next.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Strategy","What it does"],"rows":[["Sharding","Splits different data across separate machines"],["Replication","Copies the same data across separate machines"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When Sharding Becomes Necessary

blocks.alt: Data exceeding one machine points toward using sharding

blocks.text: Collections that outgrow a single machine's capacity require sharding.
Collections that comfortably fit on one machine add unneeded complexity by sharding prematurely.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Sharding a collection that would still comfortably fit on a single machine.
Choosing a shard key that overloads one machine while others remain underused.
Underestimating the network latency and coordination overhead a sharded query introduces.
Confusing sharding, which splits different data, with replication, which copies the same data.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Sharding spreads a collection's data across separate physical machines.
Partitioning splits data logically; sharding takes that split and spreads it physically.
Any single machine has a hard ceiling on memory, storage, and compute capacity.
The same shard key selection principles from partitioning apply, now with physical stakes.
A query touching multiple shards needs a coordinator to fan out and merge results.
Shards communicate over a network, adding latency a single machine search never had.
A single shard's machine failing only affects that shard's data, not the whole collection.
Sharding splits different data across machines; replication copies the same data instead.
Next up: Replication, covering how copies of the same data improve availability and reliability.
